newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. says cholera should not delay Zaire airlift.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says cholera should not delay Zaire airlift.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said on Monday an outbreak of cholera among refugees trapped by a civil war in Zaire should not delay by much the start of an airlift of 100,000 Rwandans.
Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in the northeastern city of Kisangani, said the plan was always to airlift healthy refugees first.

"I don't think it will change the timing much. We never said we wanted to start with the sick. We will allow the length of the airlift to work with the sick refugees until they are well enough to be flown out," he said.
"We hope within this week to start with small groups."

A Zairean official of the World Health Organisation (WHO) announced the epidemic on Sunday after five cholera deaths on April 7 and 8 in the Kasese 2 refugee site, 29 km (17 miles) south of Kisangani.
About 50,000 Rwandan refugees are camped out at Kasese with a similar number in makeshift camps further south.

WHO official Leonard Kinuani said the epidemic was certain to delay plans to repatriate the 100,000 refugees, who stopped months of trekking eastwards after rebels overran the area south of Kisangani.
"It appears to be a non-virulent strain which is not particularly communicable. Things seem to be stabilising. We have had 150 cases and nine deaths so far," Stromberg said.
He said the international medical aid agency Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders) was isolating suspected cholera cases and cholera kits for treatment had been flown in.

"We are distributing soap and telling people about cholera and how to avoid it. In all areas in the camps the health situation is improving," said Stromberg, adding that 93 refugees had died last Friday compared to 180 the previous Friday.
Stromberg said four aid agency planes evacuated 526 Zaireans displaced by fighting since October from Kisangani to Goma, the largest number of displaced Zaireans airlifted in Zaire so far.

"We want the two operations to go on simultaneously -- the movement of the displaced to Goma and the return of refugees," he said. He added the refugees would probably also be flown to Goma on Zaire's eastern border and trucked back into Rwanda.
The refugee airlift would be one of the biggest ever and is expected to cost millions of dollars.

Kinuani said on Sunday it might take a month to declare the refugees cholera-free. There may also be an epidemic at other refugee sites and the 10,000-strong local Zairean population was also at risk.

The refugees are the rump of more than two million Rwandan Hutus who fled their country in July 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Most returned home late last year but about 300,000 are believed to be stranded in Zaire, with the largest concentration between Kisangani and Ubundi, 125 km (75 miles) to the south.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila was put under international pressure this month to agree to the airlift after earlier insisting the refugees should be trucked home, though the roads are impassable for long stretches.

The refugees are in an appalling state after trekking about 600 km (375 miles) since last October through dense jungle where they survived on grubs and tree-bark. They marched westwards to flee Tutsi-dominated rebels, supported by Rwanda's government.
